Day 24 of 100 · Infrastructure Automation

Introduction to Ansible

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityInfrastructure AutomationTopic verified by artifact

Ansible introduced configuration management as a way to describe and repeat system changes over SSH instead of maintaining a collection of one-off login rituals.

Architecture / mental model

Control node → inventory → SSH → managed hosts → modules

How it works

Ansible is agentless for normal Linux management: the control node connects to managed hosts, gathers the information it needs and executes modules remotely.

The important shift is from typing a sequence of commands manually to describing the state you want and making that description repeatable. A playbook can be reviewed, versioned and rerun instead of living in shell history.

Inventory, authentication and privilege escalation form the path to the target. If any part of that path is wrong, automation has not failed mysteriously; a specific layer has.

Hands-on reference

ansible --version
ansible all -i inventory.ini -m ping

Verification

Run the ping module against the intended inventory and confirm every expected host responds through the exact account and SSH path you intend to automate.

Field note / gotcha

Ansible's ping module is not ICMP ping. It verifies that Ansible can connect and execute its module payload on the managed node.

Security considerations

Use SSH keys, host-key verification and controlled sudo privileges. An automation account that can become unrestricted root everywhere is convenient and correspondingly dangerous.

What I learned

Automation begins with a trustworthy control path before it begins with YAML.
